name: Interview brainteasers, set 4
description: Brainteasers of the kind interviewers ask: weighings, pirates, eggs, crossings, knockouts, invariants, hats, common knowledge and missing units. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: Twelve coins look alike, but one is a fake that is heavier or lighter. You have a balance and three weighings. You must find the fake and say whether it is heavy or light.
items.question: Which first weighing, with its plan for a level reading, always works?

options.text: Weigh 4 against 4. If level, weigh 3 of the other 4 against 3 coins now known to be genuine
Weigh 6 against 6. Whichever side moves holds the fake
options.why: You treated the fake as heavy. A tilt leaves 12 cases, 6 maybe heavy and 6 maybe light, and two weighings separate only 9.

options.text: Weigh 3 against 3. If level, the fake is among the other 6
options.why: A level reading leaves 6 coins, each heavy or light: 12 cases. Two weighings have only 9 outcomes.

options.text: Weigh 4 against 4. If level, weigh 2 of the other 4 against the other 2
options.why: If that second weighing tilts, 4 cases remain. One weighing has only 3 outcomes.

feedback.correct: Correct. 4 against 4, then 3 unknown against 3 genuine.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cases each reading leaves, and compare with 3 to the power of the weighings left.

explain.text: Every reading must leave at most 9 cases for the last two weighings. Four against four leaves 8 after a tilt and 8 after a level. Then 3 unknown against 3 genuine leaves 3, 3 or 2 cases, each settled by one weighing.

items.prose: Five pirates, A to E from the most senior, share 80 coins. The most senior alive proposes a split, and all alive vote, proposer included. A plan needs more than half the votes, or the proposer goes overboard. Each wants to survive, then coins, then to see others go overboard.
items.question: How many coins does A keep?

widget.accept: 77: A pays C 1 coin and D or E 2 coins.
widget.label: Coins A keeps

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with two pirates and work back, pricing each vote by what its owner gets if the plan fails.

byKey.tie-passes: You let a tie pass. Then B needs only one vote at four aboard, and A's votes come cheaper.
byKey.one-vote: You bought one vote. More than half of five is three, so A needs two votes besides his own.
byKey.pay-two-each: You paid both voters 2 coins. C gets nothing if A goes, so 1 coin buys C.

explain.text: With two aboard D loses E's vote, so with three C keeps 80 and D votes yes. With four, B buys D and E for 1 coin each and keeps 78. A needs two more votes: C for 1 coin and D or E for 2, so A keeps 77.

items.prose: You have three identical eggs and a 170-floor building. An egg breaks when dropped from some floor or higher, and survives below it. You must find the highest safe floor, which may be none or the top.
items.question: What is the fewest drops that always finds it?

widget.accept: 10 drops: three eggs and 10 drops settle 175 floors, 9 drops only 129.
widget.label: Fewest drops

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many floors d drops and e eggs can settle, then find the smallest d that covers 170.

byKey.nine: You stopped at 9 drops. Three eggs and 9 drops settle only 9 + 36 + 84 = 129 floors.
byKey.two-eggs: You used two eggs: 18 drops settle 171 floors. The third egg lets you take bigger steps.
byKey.halving: You halved the building each time. That needs an egg for every break, and you have only three.

explain.text: With $d$ drops and $e$ eggs you can settle $f(d, e) = f(d-1, e-1) + f(d-1, e) + 1$ floors. For three eggs that is $d + \binom{d}{2} + \binom{d}{3}$: 129 for 9 drops and 175 for 10. So 170 floors need 10 drops.

items.prose: A farmer must take a fox, a hen and a sack of grain across a river. The boat holds the farmer and one of them. Left alone together, the fox eats the hen and the hen eats the grain.
items.question: What is the fewest one-way crossings that gets everything across?

widget.accept: 7: hen over, back, fox over, hen back, grain over, back, hen over.
widget.label: Crossings

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the item that is unsafe with both others, and plan around it.

byKey.no-returns-with-cargo: You always rowed back alone. Then at some point the fox and hen, or hen and grain, are left together.
byKey.once-each: You counted one trip per item. The farmer has to row back between trips.

explain.text: The hen goes first, because the fox and the grain are safe together. Take the fox over and bring the hen back, then take the grain over. Return alone and fetch the hen: 7 crossings in all.

items.prose: Thirty-seven teams enter a knockout cup. Every match knocks one team out. A team gets a bye whenever a round has an odd number of teams.
items.question: How many matches are played, and why?

options.text: 36: each match removes one team, and 36 teams must go

options.why: You gave each team one match. The winner is never knocked out, so only 36 teams go.
You counted only the first round. The winners keep playing until one is left.

options.text: 666: every pair of teams meets once
options.why: You counted every pair, as in a league. A knockout pairs only the teams still in.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the teams that must be knocked out, not the rounds.

explain.text: Each match knocks out exactly one team. The cup ends when 36 of the 37 teams are out. So 36 matches are played, however the byes fall.

items.prose: A board holds nine numbers: 1, 1/2, 1/3 and so on down to 1/9. A move rubs out two numbers a and b and writes a + b + ab. You repeat until one number is left.
items.question: What is the last number?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a quantity the move leaves unchanged, using a + b + ab + 1.

byKey.sum: You added the numbers. Each move also adds the product ab, so the total grows.
byKey.no-minus: You found the product of the (x + 1) terms. The last number x has x + 1 equal to it, so take 1 off.

explain.text: The move keeps the product of (x + 1) fixed, because (a + 1)(b + 1) = a + b + ab + 1. At the start it is 2 × 3/2 × 4/3 × ⋯ × 10/9 = 10. The last number x has x + 1 = 10, so x = 9.

items.prose: A single pile holds 30 coins. A move splits any pile of two or more coins into two smaller piles, of any sizes. You keep making moves while you can.
items.question: Why must this end, and after how many moves?

options.text: Each move adds one pile and piles can never pass 30, so it ends after exactly 29 moves
The largest pile shrinks with every move, so it ends, but the number of moves depends on your splits
options.why: You tracked the largest pile. A move may split a small pile and leave the largest alone, and the count never varies.

options.text: Each move halves a pile, so it ends after about 5 moves
options.why: You assumed even splits. Splits can be uneven, and every way of splitting takes 29 moves.

options.text: It need not end, because a pile can be split again and again
options.why: You forgot that a pile of 1 cannot be split. The number of piles rises each move and cannot pass 30.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find a count that changes by the same amount with every move.

explain.text: The number of piles rises by exactly one with each move. It starts at 1 and can never pass 30, one coin a pile. So every game ends after exactly 29 moves, whatever you split.

items.prose: Fifteen players get red or blue hats by fair coins. Each sees every hat but their own. All at once, each guesses their own colour or passes. The team wins if someone guesses and nobody guesses wrong. They agree a plan first.
items.question: What is the team's best chance of winning? Give four decimal places.

widget.accept: 15/16 = 0.9375, from the Hamming code of length 15.
widget.label: Chance of winning

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think of a set of hat patterns the team gives up so that every other pattern wins.

byKey.one-guesser: You let one player guess and the rest pass. The others can use what they see.
byKey.three-rule: You used the answer for three players. With 15 players a longer code loses less often.
byKey.seven: That is the answer for seven players, 7/8. Fifteen players fit the next Hamming code.

explain.text: A Hamming code picks 2¹¹ of the 2¹⁵ patterns as codewords. A player guesses only when one colour would make a codeword, and names the other colour. The team then loses only on codewords: 1 − 2¹¹/2¹⁵ = 15/16 = 0.9375.

items.prose: Fifty traders share a floor, and seven have a red mark on their badge. Each sees every badge but their own, and nobody talks about marks. One morning the manager tells them all: at least one of you has a mark. Each evening, anyone sure their own badge is marked leaves. All reason perfectly.
items.question: On which evening do the marked traders leave?

widget.accept: Evening 7, one evening for each mark.
widget.label: Evening

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve it for one mark, then two, and see how the evenings grow.

byKey.seen: You counted the marks each marked trader sees. They wait one evening more to learn their own.
byKey.first: You assumed the manager's words tell each trader something new at once. Everyone already sees a mark.
byKey.late: You started counting a day late. The first evening after the words is evening 1.

explain.text: With one mark, its owner sees none and leaves on evening 1. With k marks, each owner sees k − 1 and waits for them to leave on evening k − 1. When nobody does, all k leave on evening k, so here evening 7.

items.prose: An interviewer says: "A client buys 40 at 2.5 and later sells them at 2.8. What is the profit?" Nothing else is given.
items.question: What do you ask first?

options.text: What the 40 and the prices are in: shares or lots, pounds or pence

options.why: You assumed the units. With lots of 100 shares, or prices in pence, the answer moves a hundredfold.
Fees matter, but they change the answer a little. The units can change it a hundredfold, so ask about them first.

options.text: Whether the market rose that day
options.why: The market's move does not change this trade's profit. The two prices already say what happened.

feedback.correct: Correct. Pin down the units first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which missing fact could change the answer the most.

explain.text: A number with no unit can be wrong by a factor of 100. Ask what one unit is before any arithmetic. Then give the answer with its unit: 40 × 0.3 = 12 of whatever the price is in.
